Thanks Marissa — appreciate the clear recap. A couple clarifications from our side: 

- We measure concurrency as concurrent inflight requests (not just open TCP connections). Each app server will open a small pool of persistent connections (typically 8 connections per server) but concurrency for billing/SLOs is the count of requests being processed simultaneously.
- Streaming: roughly 35% of requests use streaming. Average session length is ~2.5s, chunks every 200-300ms on average.
- Keep-alive: app servers keep connections for ~5 minutes when idle.

On quotas/rate limits: current prod traffic (pre-launch) sits around 220 r/s sustained; we plan a ramp to 500 r/s in Q2 and need headroom for marketing spikes. 

If you and infra can propose what a pilot quota looks like (target sustained + burst policy + enforcement approach), we can try the pilot for 4 weeks and measure. Also attaching our SRE email alias if infra wants to reach out: sre@acme.com.

Best,
Tom

Marissa / Lauren / Tom — quick infra take after reviewing Tom's numbers and our standard controls. TL;DR: we can run the proposed 4-week pilot with the quota bump and a couple operational safeguards. Details below.

1) Concurrency accounting: Redwood's per-customer concurrency quota measures inflight requests (request started until final token emission); connection pooling doesn't directly increase concurrency accounting, it only affects the number of TCP sessions. So ACME's definition aligns with our enforcement semantics.

2) Pilot proposal (we can roll this out next week):
- Sustained baseline: 600 r/s per region (will be enforced as a rolling window 1m average).
- Burst capacity: allow bursts to 1,200 r/s for up to 60s via token-bucket headroom. Bursts beyond that will receive 429s with Retry-After and polite-heavy metrics in console.
- Concurrency cap: soft cap at 900 inflight requests; when concurrency > 900, we will start queuing up to 150 requests per model route with a 1.5s max queue time, then shed. This keeps latency SLOs intact for the majority of short requests.
- Streaming: streaming requests count against concurrency for the duration of the session. To protect throughput we will prioritize short (non-streaming) requests in the queue during spikes; streaming clients get guaranteed minimal throughput via a small reserved token pool (5% of sustained capacity) to avoid starve-out.

3) Observability and rollback:
- We will monitor 50/ p50/p95 latencies, queue times, 429 rates, and per-route concurrency in the Redwood Console dashboards and grant ACME read-only access to the pilot workspace.
- If we observe sustained p95 latency > 350ms or 429 rate > 5% for more than a 15-minute window, we will automatically reduce burst headroom and notify both teams.

4) Operational asks from ACME:
- Confirm the region(s) you want pilot traffic routed through (us-west-2 recommended).
- Confirm contact for on-call coordination (they provided sre@acme.com — please confirm a pager).

5) Next steps:
- I'll attach a short quota spreadsheet with the exact numbers and a one-page pilot runbook (attached).
- Marissa: if that looks good, I'll schedule the pilot and we'll push the quota changes.
